comparator.sourceNotes: The 20 August 2026 adopted Dutch OER (controlling in ambiguity) and English TER, Appendix 8 pp36–37, visibly match their extracted text. For entrants from 2026, both print BA1 60 EC plus BA2/3 common requirements 60 EC, two focus areas 20 EC and minor/elective choice 35 EC: 175 itemised EC despite a stated 180-EC grand total. The preceding 2025-and-earlier section separately specifies a 5-EC research workshop and another 5-EC specialisation course; those cannot be imported selectively into the new-cohort table. Article4.5 still requires the BA2 research workshop before the thesis, but does not establish its current entrant credit allocation outside the new focus-area total. The general programme webpage retains six outgoing focus areas and a research-workshop description, without resolving the new-cohort missing credit allocation; the linked current Osiris workshop is a script-only page with no accessible formal credit/cohort detail. Its existence for current BA2 students does not settle requirements for 2026 entrants. No synthetic workshop, unnamed component or elective increment is added. The visible supported subset is175 EC, not a complete valid degree pathway.

audience.programmeDescription: IBCoM at Erasmus studies communication and media from social, cultural, political and economic perspectives, with an international and comparative approach. Students study theory and research methods, develop communication skills, undertake an internship and complete an empirical thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The confirmed communication, media, social-science and research curriculum supports these three broader UCR responses. Their different emphases concern public and cultural communication, digital media and data, and organisations and consumers. The unresolved research-workshop allocation and dependent thesis eligibility are excluded. The UCR programmes do not reproduce the full specialist methods sequence, mandatory internship or required empirical thesis.

core: Media form, cultural representation and communication in public life
Social-scientific research, quantitative and qualitative methods
Communication practice, persuasion, organisations and audiences
Media technologies, digital platforms and social consequences
questions: How do mediated representations and persuasive messages shape social life?
How do AI and digital technologies change communication and institutions?

alternatives.label: Media, culture and public communication
alternatives.concept: A programme studying media representation, persuasive communication and cultural/public life through sustained film/media inquiry, rhetorical practice, social theory and empirical methods. Organisational communication, audience research and AI ethics add specific applications; it does not reproduce a dedicated communication-science degree.
alternatives.labelReason: The label reflects the complete selected curriculum and its actual combination of media, methods and the stated complementary study; no external specialist qualification or guaranteed project topic is implied.
progression: Foundations precede advanced media/social inquiry; research methods precede advanced applications. Every formal prerequisite and planned term is checked against the current workbook.

alternatives.label: Digital media, data and society
alternatives.concept: A programme combining media/cultural analysis with computational study of images, text and data and critical inquiry into AI and digital institutions. Programming and mathematics support actual image-processing and deep-learning work; social and ethical inquiry remains substantial.
alternatives.labelReason: The label reflects the complete selected curriculum and its actual combination of media, methods and the stated complementary study; no external specialist qualification or guaranteed project topic is implied.
progression: Foundations precede advanced media/social inquiry; research methods precede advanced applications. Every formal prerequisite and planned term is checked against the current workbook.
alternatives.distinctness: Five courses change from stylistics, community rhetoric, leadership communication, media archaeology and modern social theory to mathematics, programming, image processing, neural networks and AI/institutions. This creates a computational and critical digital-media route.

alternatives.label: Media, organisational communication and consumer inquiry
alternatives.concept: A programme connecting media representation and persuasion with organisational behaviour, leadership communication, negotiation, marketing and international business. Quantitative, qualitative and market research support evidence-based communication and consumer inquiry.
alternatives.labelReason: The label reflects the complete selected curriculum and its actual combination of media, methods and the stated complementary study; no external specialist qualification or guaranteed project topic is implied.
progression: Foundations precede advanced media/social inquiry; research methods precede advanced applications. Every formal prerequisite and planned term is checked against the current workbook.
alternatives.distinctness: Six courses change from stylistics, community rhetoric, climate communication, media archaeology, television studies and youth counter-narratives to marketing, digital strategy, international business, organisational psychology, inclusive leadership and negotiation. The programme focuses on organisations and consumers rather than the first route’s cultural/public communication or the second’s computational media.

candidates.label: Media, organisational communication and consumer inquiry

selection.assessment: Three coherent feasible responses have different academic priorities. Pairwise differences are 5, 6, 8 courses respectively. Political communication is substantively covered by the closest public/cultural route through persuasion, public spheres, racial representation and counter-narratives; it is not silently left in a residual candidate. No fourth alternative is allowed.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Business & Economy in the Age of AI
trace: Film form, spectatorship, television/platforms and feminist/postcolonial interpretation directly develop media analysis.
Classical rhetorical analysis, argument, debate and speech develop direct persuasive-communication foundations.
Classical social theory, identity, networks and inequality provide the social-scientific foundations explicitly present in communication/media study.
Research design, measurement, surveys/experiments, statistical inference and regression underpin empirical communication inquiry.
Social influence, persuasion, groups and prejudice provide psychological foundations for analysing messages and audiences; the project is a proposal, not completed original research.
Community rhetorical teaching, storytelling and public-speaking practice develop specific communication skills, not the external field internship.
Leadership discourse, professional interviewing, communication advice and public-address work directly develop organisational communication.
R data cleaning, textual/tabular data and visualisation supply a concrete analytical workflow for communication research; no specialist media dataset is guaranteed.

Customer discovery, value propositions, business functions and investor pitches provide the business/consumer framework for audience research; this is complementary business study, not communication theory.
Material histories of print, optical, sound and network technologies directly examine how media infrastructures shape communication and knowledge.
Critical theory, symbolic interactionism, Bourdieu and visual case interpretation provide concrete theory for mediated culture and social power.
Interviewing, ethnography, documentary/visual approaches, reflexivity and coding supply actual qualitative research training.
Linguistic choices, discourse, ideology and narrative perspective develop textual communication analysis; literary stylistics is not a media-industry methods substitute.
Television, digital storytelling and Indigenous/disability representation directly study mediated identity and cultural power; the corpus is chiefly American.
Fairness, privacy, surveillance, trust and social effects of AI are examined through ethical and psychological inquiry, with a research-grounded podcast.
Racial construction, propaganda and marginalised storytelling are studied through historical media, archives, podcast and Photo/Voice inquiry.
Framing, coactive persuasion, ethical message design and community field research directly sustain advanced communication study.
Public spheres, hegemony, solidarity and civil movements supply advanced social theory and research directly relevant to communication as a social force.

Digital misinformation, media literacy, counter-narratives and dialogue are studied through youth extremism prevention and evidence-based communication resources; this is a specific public-communication application.
Environmental images, narratives, risk and public debate provide a specific application of media representation and ethical communication.
Documentary modes, ethics, interviewing and actual film production directly combine media analysis with research and content-making.
Analyses climate arguments across text, film, protest and social media and develops an intervention in that debate; this is a substantive communication application.
The official description supports planning and conducting market research, analysing opinions and reporting findings for business decisions; no unlisted specialist techniques are inferred.
Python programming, data structures, testing and computational problem solving supply the actual foundation for digital image/text processing.

Python/OpenCV image representation, filtering, features and recognition directly study computational handling of visual media; this is a deliberate technical extension, not an asserted external compulsory method.
Calculus, optimisation and mathematical modelling provide a specific foundation for the included neural-network and computational-media study.
AI business models, work, inequality and regulation provide specific institutional analysis of digital platforms and AI, complementing media analysis.
Neural networks, computer vision, text and transformers develop actual computational media methods with model evaluation and research; no guaranteed communication-specific project is claimed.
Organisational communication, teams, culture, power and change supply sustained organisational-behaviour inquiry, supported by research design and systematic review.
Framing, culture, trust and bargaining are applied through negotiation simulations and reflective communication analysis.
Identity safety, inclusion and emotion in leadership are investigated through an actual quantitative survey project; contributes organisational audience/interaction inquiry.
Brand identity, customer journeys, digital marketing and consumer research directly develop communication and consumer engagement.
Cross-border business, sociocultural conditions and market-entry strategy develop the international-business context of organisational communication; no global-media-system equivalence is claimed.
The official description supports strategic planning, digital business models and social responsibilities, specifically complementing organisational communication in technological change.
blocks: Both introduce media form, theory and interpretation; UCR emphasises moving images rather than the full communication-science field.
Both teach social concepts, structures, identity and inequality as foundations for social inquiry.
Public spheres, hegemony and civil movements directly address communication and collective social power; the UCR course is broader social theory.
Actual documentary planning, filming, editing and representational reflection supply a specific digital-content production relationship; not all formats are reproduced.
UCR media courses study audiences/representation but do not reproduce the primary industry-and-audience-theory overview as a separately allocated component.
Media history and business study do not establish a dedicated comparative national-media-systems course.
Cross-cultural representation and negotiation are genuine contributions but do not constitute a dedicated intercultural-communication course.
International business and cross-cultural media study do not reproduce a dedicated history/theory of international and global communication.
AI and documentary ethics are real, specific contributions but do not reproduce a dedicated communication-ethics workshop across the field.
The 10-EC restricted creative-industries/audience package is preserved as a package, not divided into invented courses or equated to one media course.
Both teach statistical description, inference and research design; UCR also includes a student research project.
Both teach qualitative inquiry, data collection and interpretation; UCR uses a broader social-research setting.
Research design is present in the statistics/research course, already aligned to statistics; no separately credited introductory social-research sequence is duplicated.
Qualitative and statistical inquiry do not reproduce this dedicated cross-national communication workshop.
Foundational statistics and applied audience research do not establish a separately credited advanced quantitative communication-methods sequence.
Leadership discourse, communication advice and public-address work directly address organisational communication practice; institutional scope differs.
Leadership communication is already aligned to communication-management practice; organisational psychology is a specific complement rather than the full corporate-communication overview.
A restricted focus-area package is retained at 10 EC; its breadth is not equated to a single UCR course.
Both examine the historical development and social effects of communication technologies; UCR adds material/artifact methods.
The identifiable overlap is AI, interaction and social/ethical consequences; UCR does not reproduce all emerging-media technologies.
UCR personal development is not a field-specific communication labour-market orientation.
Community engagement and projects are not the required 12-EC communication/media internship.
The external 15-EC empirical thesis is required; UCR optional independent research is additional to these schedules and does not certify equivalent culmination or external thesis entry.
20 EC genuine open study; no invented subject or UCR equivalence.
15 EC approved minor; its subject is not invented.

notes.text: Erasmus provides a dedicated communication-and-media curriculum with comparative media systems, international communication, field-specific research workshops, a required internship and an empirical thesis. UCR offers the broader combinations shown, with less sustained specialist communication-science training. Community projects and optional independent research do not reproduce those required external components.

acceptance.claim: The verified communication/media and social-research curriculum supports three meaningful broader UCR responses with public/cultural, computational/digital and organisational/consumer emphases; the specialist communication-science and required practical/culminating gaps remain explicit.
acceptance.targetContext: CP020, Erasmus Communication and Media (IBCoM), 2026 entrants under the 2026–2027 OER; neutral first-listed two focus areas and minor pathway.
acceptance.challengeMethod: Separately identified source-first second pass by the same AI, reading official OER/TER, current UCR evidence and finished records; not independent human or separate-agent review.

uncertainties.fact: Current-entrant allocation totals 175 EC, while Article 4.5 requires a second-year research workshop whose credit/status relationship with the new 20-EC focus allocation is unresolved.

adverseResolutions.resolution: An additional 5-EC research workshop is compulsory outside the focus allocation.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: External research preparation is stronger. UCR still supplies sustained media/persuasion inquiry and actual quantitative, qualitative, documentary and audience research; no workshop equivalence or complete research sequence is claimed.

adverseResolutions.resolution: The workshop is embedded in a restricted focus package and another 5-EC requirement or allocation correction fills the gap.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: Exact formal allocation or specialist weighting changes locally. The substantial confirmed media, communication and methods inquiry and each broader UCR response remain; the unverified requirement and relationships remain excluded.

adverseResolutions.resolution: An entrant needs additional preparation, substitution or a changed sequence for thesis entry.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: Eligibility changes, not the documented academic relationship. No waiver, completion pathway or required UCR thesis equivalence is asserted.
